planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun; Marigoule bears young and reliably and benefits from a second chestnut cultivar nearby for best pollination.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety nearby. Bred in France from a cross of European and Japanese chestnut, Marigoule combines good resistance to chestnut blight and ink disease with large, easy-to-peel nuts and a precocious habit, often bearing within a few years of planting. It has become a popular choice in North American chestnut orchards specifically because its hybrid vigor and disease tolerance let it thrive where the straight American chestnut has been devastated by blight. The tree is moderately vigorous and more compact than a full-sized American chestnut, making it a practical choice for a home orchard or food forest planting.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Carpathian strains tolerate far colder winters than typical English walnut and can be grown well outside the mild-winter regions most walnuts require.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, away from vegetable gardens and other sensitive plants since walnut roots exude juglone, a compound toxic to many other species. Carpathian refers to a cold-hardy strain of the common English (Persian) walnut originating in the mountainous Carpathian region of Poland, introduced to North America in the mid-20th century specifically because it tolerates far colder winters than typical English walnut selections from milder climates. The thin-shelled, easily cracked nuts have the classic mild, rich English walnut flavor, and the trees are large, long-lived, and productive once mature, typically beginning to bear within five to seven years of planting.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry

common_name: Thomas Black Walnut (Classic Thin-Shelled Named Black Walnut)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, well away from gardens and other juglone-sensitive plants; Thomas is grafted onto black walnut rootstock and grows into a very large shade tree over time.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, sited well away from tomatoes, apples, and other plants sensitive to the juglone this species releases into the surrounding soil. One of the oldest named black walnut cultivars, Thomas was selected in Pennsylvania in the 1880s for producing an unusually high percentage of kernel relative to shell for a species notorious for its thick, hard shell, along with the bold, distinctively rich, earthy flavor prized in baking. The tree is vigorous, cold-hardy, and eventually becomes a massive shade tree, so it is best suited to a large property or orchard edge rather than a small home garden. Nuts drop in a thick, dark, staining husk in early fall that should be removed promptly, and the tree may take eight to ten years to begin bearing from a graft.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Candy bears at a young age and requires a compatible Type I pollinator such as Pawnee or Kanza for best nut set.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety. Released by the USDA pecan breeding program, Candy is valued for bearing precociously, often producing a crop within a few years of planting, well ahead of many older commercial cultivars. Nuts are medium-sized with good kernel quality and a well-filled, attractive shell, and the tree tends to crop reliably from a young age rather than needing a long establishment period before its first real harvest. As with other pecans, supplement with zinc on alkaline soils and monitor for scab disease pressure in humid climates.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pecan Variety Selection
USDA Agricultural Research Service — Pecan Cultivar Development
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Pecan Varieties

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Schley requires a Type II pollinator such as Desirable or Elliott and is more susceptible to scab than newer disease-resistant cultivars, so it benefits from good air circulation.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety. Introduced in the early 1900s, Schley became one of the foundational commercial pecan cultivars of the 20th-century South and is still valued for its thin, easily cracked papershell and rich, high-quality kernel. It has been widely used as a parent in breeding programs that produced many of today's more disease-resistant cultivars, since it passes along excellent nut quality even though the tree itself is fairly susceptible to pecan scab in humid climates and may need fungicide protection in wet years. It remains a good choice in drier pecan-growing regions or where scab pressure is manageable.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pecan Variety Selection
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Pecan Varieties
